questions.q: What does NIST SP 800-63B recommend regarding password length versus complexity?
options: Length and complexity make no measurable difference to password strength
Require passwords to mix uppercase, lowercase, digits, and symbols above all else
Prioritize length (long passphrases) over mandatory character-mixing rules
Passwords should be as short as possible to reduce typing errors
questions.explain: Current NIST guidance favors longer passwords and passphrases over forced character-composition rules.

questions.q: Under NIST's current guidance, when should a user's password be forced to change?
options: Every single time the user logs in
Passwords should never be changed under any circumstances
Every 90 days without exception, regardless of any risk signal
Only when there's specific evidence the password has been compromised, not on a fixed calendar
questions.explain: Forced periodic rotation on a fixed schedule is no longer recommended; resets should be triggered by real evidence of compromise.

questions.q: Why did mandatory composition rules (requiring uppercase, a digit, and a symbol) fail to meaningfully improve real-world password security?
options: They pushed users toward predictable transformations of the same base word, which attackers' cracking tools already anticipate
They were only ever enforced on test accounts, never production ones
They had no effect on password length at all
They made passwords impossible for any software to check
questions.explain: Users forced into a composition rule tend to apply the same predictable substitutions (Password -> Password1! -> P@ssw0rd1!), which cracking tools already expect.

questions.q: What is breached-password screening, as described in this lesson?
options: A method for notifying users by email after a breach occurs
Requiring a password to contain at least one breached character set
Checking a candidate password against lists of passwords already exposed in real-world breaches and rejecting matches
A legacy term for mandatory 90-day password rotation
questions.explain: Services like breached-password APIs let a verifier reject any password already known to be compromised, rather than relying on complexity rules.

questions.q: Which policy combination best reflects a modern, NIST-aligned password policy for a mid-size organization?
options: Minimum 8 characters, mandatory upper/lower/digit/symbol mix, and forced rotation every 90 days
No minimum length requirement at all, and rotation every time the user changes device
Minimum 12+ characters, breached-password screening, and rotation only on confirmed compromise
Mandatory symbol requirement with no minimum length and no rotation policy of any kind
questions.explain: The lesson's example policy replaces the old 8-character/complexity/90-day-rotation model with longer minimum length, breach screening, and compromise-triggered rotation.
